description: HEAMON is a health monitoring device designed to track and record an individual's vital signs in real time. It provides visibility into key cardiovascular health indicators—such as heart rate, blood pressure, and other physiological parameters—facilitating continuous health monitoring and contributing to the timely detection of potential abnormalities.
summary: The system proposes using remote photoplethysmography (rPPG)—a technique that seeks to extract, from video, subtle color variations associated with the blood pulse. Based on this signal, the project aims to: identify the facial region of interest; extract an approximate pulse wave; filter out noise, motion, and respiratory variations; segment the signal into temporal windows; generate features derived from the pulse wave; employ a neural network to estimate systolic and diastolic blood pressure; visualize results, signal quality, and metrics; allow for individual calibration using a reference reading; and estimate anthropometric measurements based on deviations in the data. The value of this approach lies not merely in “measuring blood pressure with a camera”—a claim that remains to be fully proven—but in exploring a lightweight, reusable, non-invasive tool that could potentially be operated on-board for physiological monitoring.
details:
1. Heart Rate: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) to estimate heart rate using facial video. Blood Pressure: Deep learning-based estimation, currently undergoing testing and validation. Respiratory Monitoring: Computer vision techniques to analyze respiratory patterns. Visual Fatigue: Eye-related features and visual behavior analysis. Anthropometry: Image-based estimation of body dimensions and proportions.
  2. Remote Photoplethysmography (rPPG) is a non-contact technique that uses a conventional camera to detect subtle changes in skin color caused by variations in blood volume with each heartbeat. When the heart pumps blood, blood flow through facial blood vessels changes periodically. These variations produce tiny changes in the amount of light reflected by the skin. By recording facial video and analyzing changes in RGB color channels, the system extracts a periodic physiological signal. This signal can then be processed to estimate heart rate without requiring physical contact or traditional sensors.
